title: Consistency & Failure Handling
description: Explore tunable consistency with quorum reads/writes, gossip protocol for cluster membership, Merkle trees for anti-entropy, and hinted handoff for temporary failures.

segments.text: A key-value store that runs on a single machine is easy. The hard part is making it distributed, fault-tolerant, and tunable. Today we'll cover the four mechanisms that make a distributed key-value store production-ready: tunable consistency, gossip, Merkle trees, and hinted handoff.

Remember R plus W greater than N from our replication lesson? In a key-value store, you let clients choose their consistency level per request. Want strong consistency? Set R equals 2 and W equals 2 with N equals 3. Want fast reads? Set R equals 1 and W equals 3.

Cassandra exposes this beautifully. Consistency level ONE reads from any single replica — fast but potentially stale. QUORUM reads from a majority. ALL reads from every replica — slowest but guaranteed fresh. You choose per query based on the use case.
segments.thought_prompt: When would you choose consistency level ONE over QUORUM?

segments.text: How does each node know which other nodes are alive and what data they own? The gossip protocol. Periodically, each node picks a random peer and exchanges membership information. Like rumors in a school, information spreads exponentially and reaches everyone quickly.

Gossip is decentralized — no single coordinator can fail. It's eventually consistent — all nodes converge to the same view. And it scales well — each node only talks to a few peers each round, yet information propagates in O of log N rounds. Perfect for cluster membership.

Over time, replicas can drift. Network partitions, failed writes, software bugs — they all cause replicas to diverge. How do you detect and fix these inconsistencies without comparing every single key? Merkle trees make this efficient.

Each node builds a hash tree over its data. Leaf nodes are hashes of individual key ranges. Parent nodes are hashes of their children. Two replicas compare their root hashes. If they match, all data is identical. If not, they traverse down the tree to find exactly which key ranges differ.
segments.thought_prompt: How much data do two replicas need to exchange to find which keys are different?

segments.text: The beauty is efficiency. Instead of comparing millions of keys, you compare O of log N hashes to pinpoint the inconsistent ranges. Then you only sync those specific ranges. DynamoDB and Cassandra both use Merkle trees for this anti-entropy repair process.

When a replica is temporarily down during a write, hinted handoff saves the day. Another node stores the write as a 'hint' — a note saying 'deliver this to node C when it comes back.' When node C recovers, the hints are replayed, and no data is lost.

Hinted handoff enables sloppy quorums. Normally W equals 2 means writing to 2 of the 3 designated replicas. With sloppy quorum, if one designated replica is down, write to any available node instead. Availability increases at the cost of temporary inconsistency.

These four mechanisms work together. Tunable consistency lets clients choose their trade-offs. Gossip keeps the cluster aware of itself. Merkle trees repair drift in the background. And hinted handoff ensures writes survive temporary outages. Together, they make distributed key-value stores resilient.
